section: 1.1 Theories and Mechanisms of Pain
text: 1.1.1 Understand contemporary and evolving theories of pain, their historical context, and their relative usefulness in clinical practice. 1.1.2 Understand the philosophical aspects of pain theory (such as monism versus dualism; reductionism versus holism; and embodied predictive processing). 1.1.3 Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of the transduction, transmission, perception and modulation of nociception and pain including: The characteristics of sensory neurons (e.g., C-fibres and A-fibres). Relevant pathways, structures, receptors, ion-channels, and neurotransmitters. 1.1.4 Discuss the distinction between nociception and pain. 1.1.5 Discuss mechanistic descriptors and classifications of pain (such as 'nociceptive', 'neuropathic' and 'nociplastic' pain) and their relevance to the assessment and management of patients' pain. 1.1.6 Understand the concepts and neurobiological mechanisms underlying peripheral and central sensitisation, primary and secondary hyperalgesia, and the transition from acute to chronic pain.

section: 1.2 The Language of Pain Science
text: 1.2.1 Understand common pain and neuroscience-related phenomena as defined by the IASP terminology (e.g., hyperalgesia, allodynia, sensitisation) and the World Health Organisation (WHO, e.g., ICD-11, ICF). 1.2.2 Understand other contemporary pain-related terminologies (e.g., lived experience of pain, stigmatisation, person-centeredness, and diagnostic uncertainty).

section: 1.3 The Complex, Variable and Multidimensional Nature of Pain
text: 1.3.1 Discuss the pain science underlying the complexity, variability, and multidimensionality of pain: Evolution, application, and limitations of the biopsychosocial model of pain. Aspects of a lived-experience of pain and how the person in pain can be included in the process of assessment and management. Cognitive dimensions of pain (pain-related beliefs, experiences, self-stigmatisation, fear-avoidance, catastrophizing, operant and classical conditioning). Role of lifestyle factors on nociception and pain (physical activity/inactivity, obesity, sleep, substance misuse, stress, trauma/violence). Modifiable and non-modifiable risk factors linked to the development of chronic pain (genetic, socioeconomic, occupational, educational factors, multimorbidity, emotional wellbeing, health literacy, social stigmatisation). Role of contextual factors on pain (placebo, nocebo, therapeutic alliance, healthcare culture). ---

section: 2.1 Assessment
text: 2.1.1 Demonstrate the ability to plan and undertake a comprehensive assessment of the person in pain across the lifespan using a biopsychosocial and person-centred approach. 2.1.2 Discuss the rationale behind basic biopsychosocial assessment of a person in pain. 2.1.3 Demonstrate an understanding of how cultural, societal, economic and institutional environments may influence pain assessment. 2.1.4 Demonstrate an understanding of patient and provider factors (e.g., attitudes, beliefs, values, health literacy, affective, cognitive, behavioural responses) that may influence pain assessment. 2.1.5 Demonstrate a person-centred approach that considers biological, functional, psychological, work-related and social aspects of the person in pain. 2.1.6 Demonstrate knowledge of the rationale for and value of basic investigations (such as red flags, serious pathology, neuropathies, musculoskeletal injuries). 2.1.7 Understand the role of specialist assessment, and when it is appropriate to refer for investigation and multidisciplinary / medical management.

section: 2.2 Outcome Measures
text: 2.2.1 Demonstrate an ability to select and interpret valid and reliable pain-specific biopsychosocial outcome measures across the ICF domains to assess, monitor, and modify treatment. 2.2.2 Demonstrate ability to undertake physical assessment (levels of physical activity, function in daily life, functional tests, capacity evaluations, sleep). 2.2.3 Demonstrate an understanding of, and ability to select, valid and reliable tools to monitor the effect of pain management interventions across the lifespan and in special populations (pediatric, older adults, cognitive impairment, cultural/linguistic diversity). ---

section: 3.1 Foundations of Treatment
text: 3.1.1 Demonstrate the professional responsibility of treating all patients with dignity and respect, irrespective of background and status. 3.1.2 Develop, justify, and negotiate with the patient an individually tailored treatment plan based on evidence, clinical reasoning, and patient preferences. 3.1.3 Understand and apply the principles of evidence-based practice and research when planning and implementing treatment. 3.1.4 Discuss the importance of proactively, systematically, and continually evaluating pain management outcomes. 3.1.5 Understand and differentiate between multimodal and multidisciplinary pain management.

section: 3.2 Treatment Effects
text: 3.2.1 Understand the range of treatment effects and outcomes that can occur (positive, negative, adverse, unpredicted, nocebo/placebo, specific vs non-specific). 3.2.2 Understand the balance of treatment effects and side-effects.

section: 3.3 Communication
text: 3.3.1 Demonstrate the ability to communicate empathetically, respectfully, and effectively with people in pain and significant others. 3.3.2 Apply communication strategies to facilitate shared decision-making, patient self-efficacy, and therapeutic alliance. 3.3.3 Formulate and discuss a prognosis and realistic goals with patients.

section: 3.4 Education
text: 3.4.1 Demonstrate ability to use contemporary science-based explanations (e.g., neurophysiology / PNE) with patients and carers. 3.4.2 Provide and discuss appropriate information about a range of pain management interventions. 3.4.3 Awareness of service delivery modes (online, group education, 1-on-1). 3.4.4 Apply educational strategies that enhance health literacy, active engagement, and supported self-management.

section: 3.5 Behavioural Therapies
text: 3.5.1 Demonstrate knowledge of behavioural therapies (CBT, ACT, MBSR, relaxation, autogenic training, graded exposure, graded activity). 3.5.2 Identify psychological risk factors (Yellow Flags) and adapt physiotherapy treatment accordingly.

section: 3.6 Physical Activity and Exercise Prescription
text: 3.6.1 Demonstrate and apply evidence-based physical activity and exercise prescription in chronic pain. 3.6.2 Understand barriers and health benefits of physical activity for people in pain. 3.6.3 Modify physical activity based on pain state, age, comorbidities, pregnancy, dementia, mental health issues.

section: 3.7 Digital Health Management
text: 3.7.1 Discuss opportunities, limitations, and ethical issues associated with digital health technologies (apps, wearables, telehealth, virtual reality).

section: 3.8 Work
text: 3.8.1 Understand the importance of work for physical, psychological, and financial health. 3.8.2 Discuss factors influencing work capability, absence, and return-to-work (Blue and Black flags). 3.8.3 Apply return-to-work strategies in collaboration with patients and employers.

section: 3.9 Referral & Multidisciplinary Collaboration
text: 3.9.1 Collaborate across multidisciplinary teams in health and social care. 3.9.2 Understand indications, efficacy, complications, and evidence for procedural modalities (injections, surgery, neuromodulation/SCS). 3.9.3 Demonstrate knowledge of analgesic pharmacological classes (indications, mechanisms, side-effects, interactions with exercise, opioid-induced hyperalgesia). ---

section: 4.1 Epidemiology
text: 4.1.1 Demonstrate knowledge of epidemiology of chronic pain (incidence, prevalence, societal impact). 4.1.2 Understand socio-demographic factors (age, gender, ethnicity, socioeconomic status) on health inequalities. 4.1.3 Understand risk, prognostic, and predictive factors for the transition from acute to chronic pain.

section: 4.2 Pain Assessment and Management for Specific Populations
text: 4.2.1 Adapt assessment and management across life stages (infants, children, adolescents, working age, older adults). 4.2.2 Specific clinical conditions: Musculoskeletal pain (spinal, peripheral joint, tendinopathy, myofascial). Osteoarthritis. Inflammatory and autoimmune arthropathies. Chronic widespread pain / Fibromyalgia. Chronic post-surgical and post-traumatic pain. Complex Regional Pain Syndrome (CRPS). Neuropathic pain (peripheral and central). Pelvic pain conditions. Headache and orofacial pain. Cancer-related pain. Visceral pain. 4.2.3 Vulnerable groups (cognitive impairment / dementia, non-communicative patients, trauma/torture survivors, addiction/substance use). ---

section: 5.1 Interprofessional Working and Learning
text: 5.1.1 Discuss the importance of interprofessional working along with barriers and facilitators. 5.1.2 Work in partnership with patients, carers, multidisciplinary team members and agencies. 5.1.3 Engage in regular interprofessional education, peer supervision, and reflective practice.

section: IASP Taxonomy & Pain Definitions — Authoritative Master Sheet (EFIC Diploma)
text: > Official Standard: International Association for the Study of Pain (IASP) Terminology & Taxonomy Revision. > Rule for the EFIC Exam: Questions testing definitions require EXACT VERBATIM KNOWLEDGE of the clauses (e.g. "whether spontaneous or evoked" , "associated with, or resembling" , "non-neural tissue" , "somatosensory nervous system" ). ---

section: 1. Pain
text: Official IASP Definition (VERBATIM): > "An unpleasant sensory and emotional experience associated with, or resembling that associated with, actual or potential tissue damage." Official IASP Commentary & Clinical Notes: 1. Pain is always a personal experience influenced by biological, psychological, and social factors. 2. Pain and nociception are different phenomena. 3. Through life experiences, individuals learn the concept of pain. 4. A person's report of an experience as pain should be respected. 5. Although pain usually serves an adaptive role, it may have adverse effects on function and well-being. 6. Verbal description is only one behavior to express pain; inability to communicate does not negate the possibility of experiencing pain. ⚠️ Exam Distractor Trap: Distractor will omit 'emotional', claim pain requires 'actual tissue damage' (omitting 'potential' or 'resembling'), or claim non-verbal patients cannot experience pain. ---

section: 2. Allodynia
text: Official IASP Definition (VERBATIM): > "Pain due to a stimulus that does not normally provoke pain." Official IASP Commentary & Clinical Notes: Note that the stimulus leads to an unexpectedly painful response. This is a clinical term that does not imply a mechanism. The stimulus and response mode differ (i.e. non-painful stimulus produces painful response). ⚠️ Exam Distractor Trap: Distractor will swap with hyperalgesia: claiming allodynia is 'exaggerated pain to a noxious stimulus'. ---

section: 3. Hyperalgesia
text: Official IASP Definition (VERBATIM): > "Increased pain from a stimulus that normally provokes pain." Official IASP Commentary & Clinical Notes: Current evidence suggests that hyperalgesia is a consequence of perturbation of the nociceptive system with peripheral or central sensitization, or both. The stimulus and response mode are the same (i.e. painful stimulus produces magnified pain). ⚠️ Exam Distractor Trap: Distractor will define it as pain provoked by a non-painful stimulus. ---

section: 4. Dysesthesia
text: Official IASP Definition (VERBATIM): > "An unpleasant abnormal sensation, whether spontaneous or evoked." Official IASP Commentary & Clinical Notes: Compare with paresthesia. A dysesthesia should always be unpleasant, and a paresthesia should not be unpleasant. It should always be specified whether the sensations are spontaneous or evoked. ⚠️ Exam Distractor Trap: Distractor will say dysesthesia is 'only evoked by touch' or omit the word 'unpleasant'. ---

section: 5. Paresthesia
text: Official IASP Definition (VERBATIM): > "An abnormal sensation, whether spontaneous or evoked." Official IASP Commentary & Clinical Notes: Compare with dysesthesia. A paresthesia should not be unpleasant (e.g. tingling, pins and needles). It should always be specified whether the sensations are spontaneous or evoked. ⚠️ Exam Distractor Trap: Distractor will state paresthesia is inherently painful or unpleasant. ---

section: 6. Nociceptive Pain
text: Official IASP Definition (VERBATIM): > "Pain that arises from actual or threatened damage to non-neural tissue and is due to the activation of nociceptors." Official IASP Commentary & Clinical Notes: Used to describe pain occurring with a normally functioning somatosensory nervous system, to contrast with the abnormal function seen in neuropathic pain. ⚠️ Exam Distractor Trap: Distractor will categorize radiculopathy or fibromyalgia as nociceptive pain. ---

section: 7. Neuropathic Pain
text: Official IASP Definition (VERBATIM): > "Pain caused by a lesion or disease of the somatosensory nervous system." Official IASP Commentary & Clinical Notes: Requires a demonstrable lesion or disease that satisfies established neurological diagnostic criteria with neuroanatomical plausibility. ⚠️ Exam Distractor Trap: Distractor will claim somatic referred pain or muscle spasm pain is neuropathic. ---

section: 8. Nociplastic Pain
text: Official IASP Definition (VERBATIM): > "Pain that arises from altered nociception despite no clear evidence of actual or threatened tissue damage causing the activation of peripheral nociceptors or evidence for disease or lesion of the somatosensory system causing the pain." Official IASP Commentary & Clinical Notes: Clinical features include multifocal/widespread pain, hypersensitivity (allodynia, hyperalgesia), fatigue, sleep, and cognitive disturbance (e.g. fibromyalgia). ⚠️ Exam Distractor Trap: Distractor will call it 'psychogenic pain' or claim it involves a structural nerve lesion. ---

section: 9. Nociception
text: Official IASP Definition (VERBATIM): > "The neural process of encoding noxious stimuli." Official IASP Commentary & Clinical Notes: Consequences may be autonomic or behavioral. Pain perception is not necessarily implied. Nociception != pain. ⚠️ Exam Distractor Trap: Distractor will claim nociception is synonymous with pain or that pain cannot exist without nociception. ---

section: 10. Nociceptor
text: Official IASP Definition (VERBATIM): > "A high-threshold sensory receptor of the peripheral somatosensory nervous system that is capable of transducing and encoding noxious stimuli." Official IASP Commentary & Clinical Notes: Includes A-delta and C primary afferent nerve endings. ⚠️ Exam Distractor Trap: Distractor will call nociceptors 'pain receptors' (receptors transduce energy, they do not feel pain). ---

section: 11. Nociceptive Neuron
text: Official IASP Definition (VERBATIM): > "A central or peripheral neuron of the somatosensory nervous system that is capable of encoding noxious stimuli." Official IASP Commentary & Clinical Notes: Can be peripheral or central (e.g. dorsal horn Wide Dynamic Range or nociceptive-specific neurons). ⚠️ Exam Distractor Trap: Distractor will claim nociceptive neurons are only found in the peripheral nervous system. ---

section: 12. Nociceptive Stimulus
text: Official IASP Definition (VERBATIM): > "An actually or potentially tissue-damaging event transduced and encoded by nociceptors." Official IASP Commentary & Clinical Notes: Refers to the physical stimulus acting on nociceptors. ⚠️ Exam Distractor Trap: Distractor will confuse stimulus with sensation. ---

section: 13. Noxious Stimulus
text: Official IASP Definition (VERBATIM): > "An actually or potentially tissue-damaging event." Official IASP Commentary & Clinical Notes: May be mechanical, thermal, or chemical. ⚠️ Exam Distractor Trap: Distractor will claim non-noxious stimuli can activate normal nociceptors. ---

section: 14. Analgesia
text: Official IASP Definition (VERBATIM): > "Absence of pain in response to stimulation which would normally be painful." Official IASP Commentary & Clinical Notes: Encompasses pharmacological analgesia, congenital insensitivity to pain, or nerve block. ⚠️ Exam Distractor Trap: Distractor will confuse analgesia (absence of pain to noxious stimulus) with anesthesia (absence of all sensation). ---

section: 15. Anesthesia Dolorosa
text: Official IASP Definition (VERBATIM): > "Pain in an area or region which is anesthetic." Official IASP Commentary & Clinical Notes: Typically seen after deafferentation or surgical lesioning (e.g. trigeminal rhizotomy). ⚠️ Exam Distractor Trap: Distractor will claim an anesthetic area cannot feel pain. ---

section: 16. Central Pain
text: Official IASP Definition (VERBATIM): > "Pain initiated or caused by a primary lesion or disease of the central somatosensory nervous system." Official IASP Commentary & Clinical Notes: Examples: post-stroke thalamic pain, spinal cord injury pain, multiple sclerosis pain. ⚠️ Exam Distractor Trap: Distractor will categorize central sensitization in fibromyalgia as 'central pain' (central pain requires a lesion/disease of CNS somatosensory tracts). ---

section: 17. Peripheral Neuropathic Pain
text: Official IASP Definition (VERBATIM): > "Pain caused by a lesion or disease of the peripheral somatosensory nervous system." Official IASP Commentary & Clinical Notes: Examples: painful diabetic polyneuropathy, post-herpetic neuralgia, radiculopathy. ⚠️ Exam Distractor Trap: Distractor will include musculoskeletal pain radiating into the limb. ---

section: 18. Central Sensitization
text: Official IASP Definition (VERBATIM): > "Increased responsiveness of nociceptive neurons in the central nervous system to their normal or subthreshold afferent input." Official IASP Commentary & Clinical Notes: Includes dorsal horn and supraspinal amplification and loss of descending inhibition. Peripheral neurons are typically not involved in this definition. ⚠️ Exam Distractor Trap: Distractor will claim central sensitization is caused by peripheral nociceptor membrane phosphorylation. ---

section: 19. Peripheral Sensitization
text: Official IASP Definition (VERBATIM): > "Increased responsiveness and reduced threshold of nociceptive neurons in the periphery to the stimulation of their receptive fields." Official IASP Commentary & Clinical Notes: Driven by inflammatory soup (prostaglandins, bradykinin, NGF) sensitizing ion channels (TRPV1, Nav1.7/1.8). ⚠️ Exam Distractor Trap: Distractor will claim peripheral sensitization causes secondary hyperalgesia (it causes primary hyperalgesia). ---

section: 20. Sensitization
text: Official IASP Definition (VERBATIM): > "Increased responsiveness of nociceptive neurons to their normal input, and/or recruitment of a response to normally subthreshold inputs." Official IASP Commentary & Clinical Notes: Umbrella neurophysiological term encompassing both peripheral and central sensitization. ⚠️ Exam Distractor Trap: Distractor will say sensitization refers to psychological distress. ---

section: 21. Hyperpathia
text: Official IASP Definition (VERBATIM): > "A painful syndrome characterized by an abnormally painful reaction to a stimulus, especially a repetitive stimulus, as well as an increased threshold." Official IASP Commentary & Clinical Notes: Faulty identification/localization, delay in perception, radiating sensation, and explosive character outlasting stimulus are hallmarks. ⚠️ Exam Distractor Trap: Distractor will claim hyperpathia has a lowered initiation threshold (the threshold is ELEVATED/INCREASED!). ---

section: 22. Hyperesthesia
text: Official IASP Definition (VERBATIM): > "Increased sensitivity to stimulation, excluding the special senses." Official IASP Commentary & Clinical Notes: Encompasses both allodynia and hyperalgesia, but also refers to non-painful touch and thermal modalities. ⚠️ Exam Distractor Trap: Distractor will claim hyperesthesia only applies to painful sensations. ---

section: 23. Hypoesthesia
text: Official IASP Definition (VERBATIM): > "Decreased sensitivity to stimulation, excluding the special senses." Official IASP Commentary & Clinical Notes: Refers to cutaneous modalities (touch, warmth, cold). ⚠️ Exam Distractor Trap: Distractor will confuse hypoesthesia (decreased sensation) with hypoalgesia (decreased pain). ---

section: 24. Hypoalgesia
text: Official IASP Definition (VERBATIM): > "Diminished pain in response to a normally painful stimulus." Official IASP Commentary & Clinical Notes: Refers specifically to noxious/painful stimuli. ⚠️ Exam Distractor Trap: Distractor will claim hypoalgesia is the complete absence of pain (that is analgesia). ---

section: 25. Neuralgia
text: Official IASP Definition (VERBATIM): > "Pain in the distribution of a nerve or nerves." Official IASP Commentary & Clinical Notes: E.g. Trigeminal neuralgia, glossopharyngeal neuralgia, occipital neuralgia. ⚠️ Exam Distractor Trap: Distractor will claim neuralgia requires pathological inflammation (that is neuritis). ---

section: 26. Neuritis
text: Official IASP Definition (VERBATIM): > "Inflammation of a nerve or nerves." Official IASP Commentary & Clinical Notes: Reserved for processes which are inflammatory; should not be used for degenerative conditions unless inflammation is also present. ⚠️ Exam Distractor Trap: Distractor will call any nerve compression or neuropathy 'neuritis'. ---

section: 27. Neuropathy
text: Official IASP Definition (VERBATIM): > "A disturbance of function or pathological change in a nerve: in one nerve, mononeuropathy; in several nerves, mononeuropathy multiplex; if diffuse and bilateral, polyneuropathy." Official IASP Commentary & Clinical Notes: Non-inflammatory structural or functional nerve disorder. ⚠️ Exam Distractor Trap: Distractor will require pain for neuropathy (neuropathy can be purely painless motor or sensory loss). ---

section: 28. Pain Threshold
text: Official IASP Definition (VERBATIM): > "The minimum intensity of a stimulus that is perceived as painful." Official IASP Commentary & Clinical Notes: Traditionally the lowest stimulus intensity at which a subject perceives pain in 50% of trials. Represents a sensory-discriminative endpoint. ⚠️ Exam Distractor Trap: Distractor will state pain threshold reflects psychological coping. ---

section: 29. Pain Tolerance Level
text: Official IASP Definition (VERBATIM): > "The maximum intensity of a pain-producing stimulus that a subject is willing to accept in a given situation." Official IASP Commentary & Clinical Notes: Heavily influenced by cognitive, motivational, cultural, and contextual factors. ⚠️ Exam Distractor Trap: Distractor will claim pain tolerance is a fixed physiological spinal reflex. ---

section: 30. Causalgia
text: Official IASP Definition (VERBATIM): > "A syndrome of sustained burning pain, allodynia, and hyperpathia after a traumatic nerve lesion, often combined with vasomotor and sudomotor dysfunction and later trophic changes." Official IASP Commentary & Clinical Notes: Historically known as Reflex Sympathetic Dystrophy / now classified as Complex Regional Pain Syndrome Type II (CRPS II). ⚠️ Exam Distractor Trap: Distractor will say causalgia occurs without a nerve injury (CRPS Type I occurs without nerve injury; Causalgia / Type II requires a nerve lesion). ---

section: 31. Neurogenic Pain
text: Official IASP Definition (VERBATIM): > "Pain initiated or caused by a primary lesion, dysfunction, or transitory perturbation in the peripheral or central nervous system." Official IASP Commentary & Clinical Notes: An older term largely superseded by 'neuropathic pain' (for lesions) and 'nociplastic pain' (for dysfunction). ⚠️ Exam Distractor Trap: Distractor will treat neurogenic and neuropathic pain as strictly identical in modern taxonomy. ---

section: A. Allodynia vs. Hyperalgesia (The Core Distinction)
text: Attribute Allodynia Hyperalgesia --- --- --- Exact Definition "Pain due to a stimulus that does not normally provoke pain." "Increased pain from a stimulus that normally provokes pain." Stimulus Mode Non-noxious (innocuous brush, cotton wisp, clothing, mild warm/cold). Noxious (pinprick, sharp probe, heat >45°C). Response Pain elicited where none should exist. Pain exaggerated in intensity and/or duration. IASP Rule Stimulus and response mode differ (touch \rightarrow pain). Stimulus and response mode are the same (pain \rightarrow extreme pain). Clinical Subtypes Dynamic mechanical ( A\beta brush), Static/Punctate, Thermal. Primary (peripheral / zone of injury) vs. Secondary (central / undamaged zone).

section: B. Dysesthesia vs. Paresthesia (The Unpleasantness Rule)
text: Attribute Paresthesia Dysesthesia --- --- --- Exact Definition "An abnormal sensation, whether spontaneous or evoked." "An unpleasant abnormal sensation, whether spontaneous or evoked." Unpleasantness NOT unpleasant (by definition). STRICTLY unpleasant / distressing . Triggering Mode Whether spontaneous or evoked (can be either). Whether spontaneous or evoked (can be either). Examples Tingling, "limb falling asleep", vibration, non-painful pins & needles. Burning tingling, painful crawling, painful cold/freezing, electric buzzing.

section: C. The 3 Mechanistic Pain Types (Kosek et al. 2016 / 2021)
text: Parameter Nociceptive Pain Neuropathic Pain Nociplastic Pain --- --- --- --- Verbatim Definition "Pain that arises from actual or threatened damage to non-neural tissue and is due to the activation of nociceptors." "Pain caused by a lesion or disease of the somatosensory nervous system." "Pain that arises from altered nociception despite no clear evidence of actual or threatened tissue damage... or evidence for disease or lesion of the somatosensory system." Somatosensory System Normally functioning nervous system. Structural/pathological lesion or disease in somatosensory tracts. Structurally intact; functional central amplification/loss of inhibition. Key Clinical Trap Cannot involve non-neural tissue. Somatic referred pain radiating down leg is NOT neuropathic. Not psychogenic; real neurobiological altered nociceptive processing.

section: Section 1: Pain Science and Knowledge — EFIC Ingest & Study Guide
text: This module covers the core theoretical, biological, philosophical, and systemic foundations required for Section One: Pain Science and Knowledge of the official EFIC Core Curriculum. ---

section: A. Philosophical Foundations & Epistemic Frameworks (1.1.2)
text: - Cartesian Dualism (René Descartes, 1664): - Conceptualized pain as a direct, mechanical pull on a string leading from the damaged tissue (e.g., foot in fire) directly to an alarm bell in the brain. - Philosophical Flaw: Strict separation of Mind ( res cogitans ) and Body ( res extensa ). Leads to the false biomedical dichotomy: "pain is either organic (tissue injury) or psychogenic (in the head)" . - Curriculum Rebuttal: Dualism fails because pain is non-linear, centrally modulated, and inherently biopsychosocial. - Monism vs. Dualism: - Monism (Physicalism / Identity Theory): Mind and brain are one biological continuum; subjective experiences of pain arise from physical neural processing without requiring an immaterial soul. - Enactive / Embodied Cognition (4E Cognition): Pain is not merely an internal neural representation, but an embodied, embedded, enacted, and extended sense-making process of the whole organism interacting with its physical and social environment. - Reductionism vs. Biopsychosocial Holism (George Engel, 1977): - Biomedical Reductionism: Assumes all pain can be reduced to nociceptive input, mechanical tissue fault, or biochemical pathology. - Biopsychosocial Holism: Biological nociception is filtered through, modulated by, and inseparable from psychological appraisals (meaning, catastrophizing, fear) and sociocultural contexts (workplace, disability policy, relationships, marginalization). - Epistemic Injustice & Pain Validation (Fricker / EFIC Curricul

section: B. Evolution of Theoretical Models in Pain Science (1.1.1)
text: 1. Specificity Theory (von Frey, 1894): Hypothesized dedicated pain receptors and distinct pathways directly to a pain center in the brain. Overturned because it cannot explain central modulation, phantom pain, or allodynia. 2. Pattern Theory (Goldscheider, 1894): Proposed that pain results from spatial and temporal summation of non-specific somatic receptors. Incomplete, but anticipated summation mechanisms. 3. Gate Control Theory (Melzack & Wall, 1965): - Located in the substantia gelatinosa (Lamina II of the spinal dorsal horn). - Large-diameter non-nociceptive A\beta fibers activate inhibitory interneurons, "closing the gate" to spinal transmission ( T ) cells. - Small A\delta and C nociceptive fibers inhibit the inhibitory interneurons, "opening the gate" . - Incorporates descending top-down modulation from cortical and brainstem structures (attention, emotion, anticipation). 4. Neuromatrix Theory of Pain (Ronald Melzack, 1999): - Pain is produced by a widely distributed brain neural network (the body-self neuromatrix ) comprising: - Sensory-discriminative dimension ( S1, S2 , lateral thalamus). - Affective-motivational dimension (limbic system, anterior insula, ACC, amygdala). - Cognitive-evaluative dimension (prefrontal cortices, posterior parietal cortex). - Generates a characteristic neurochemical/neural output called a neurosignature . section: A. Primary Afferents & Peripheral Sensors (1.1.3)
text: - Primary Afferent Classes: - A\beta fibers: Large diameter ( 6\text{–}12\ \mu\text{m} ), heavily myelinated, rapid conduction velocity ( 30\text{–}70\text{ m/s} ). Low-threshold mechanoreceptors (light touch, vibration, proprioception). Normally non-nociceptive; during central sensitization, can activate T -cells via phenotypic switching / disinhibition to trigger dynamic mechanical allodynia . - A\delta fibers: Medium diameter ( 1\text{–}5\ \mu\text{m} ), lightly myelinated, intermediate conduction velocity ( 5\text{–}30\text{ m/s} ). High-threshold mechanoreceptors and mechano-thermal nociceptors. Mediate "first pain" (sharp, well-localized, rapid pricking pain; triggers withdrawal reflex). - C fibers: Small diameter ( 0.2\text{–}1.5\ \mu\text{m} ), unmyelinated, slow conduction velocity ( 0.5\text{–}2\text{ m/s} ). Mediate "second pain" (dull, burning, diffuse, prolonged aching pain). - Subclasses of C -Fibers (Crucial for EFIC MCQ): - Peptidergic C -fibers: - Express TrkA (Nerve Growth Factor / NGF high-affinity receptor). - Contain neuropeptides: Substance P and Calcitonin Gene-Related Peptide (CGRP) . - Mediate neurogenic inflammation via antidromic axon reflex: CGRP causes profound arteriolar vasodilation (flare), while Substance P causes vascular permeability and plasma extravasation (wheal/edema). - Non-peptidergic C -fibers: - Bind isolectin B4 ( IB4 ), express purinergic receptors ( P2X 3 ), and Ret (GDNF receptor). Do not produce classic neurogenic flare. - C -Ta

section: B. Spinal Dorsal Horn Laminae & Ascending Tracts
text: - Rexed Laminae Architecture: - Lamina I (Marginal Zone): Receives direct nociceptive input from A\delta and peptidergic C fibers. Contains nociceptive-specific (NS) projection neurons. - Lamina II (Substantia Gelatinosa): Dense network of excitatory and inhibitory (GABAergic / glycinergic) interneurons. Essential site of Gate Control. - Lamina III & IV (Nucleus Proprius): Receive primarily non-noxious A\beta inputs (touch, pressure). - Lamina V: Contains Wide Dynamic Range (WDR) neurons . WDR neurons receive convergent monosynaptic inputs from A\beta , A\delta , and polysynaptic inputs from C fibers, as well as visceral afferents (anatomical basis for viscerosomatic referred pain ). WDR neurons undergo wind-up. - Ascending Tracts: - Spinothalamic Tract (STT): - Lateral STT: Projects to ventral posterolateral (VPL) and ventral posteromedial (VPM) nuclei of the thalamus \rightarrow S1 and S2 . Encodes sensory-discriminative dimensions (location, intensity, duration, quality). - Medial STT: Projects to medial thalamic nuclei (central lateral, parafascicular) \rightarrow Anterior Cingulate Cortex (ACC) and insula. Encodes affective-motivational dimensions. - Spinoreticular Tract: Projects to brainstem reticular formation (mediates motor arousal, autonomic reflexes, and sleep disruption). - Spinomesencephalic Tract: Projects to the Periaqueductal Gray (PAG) to engage endogenous descending feedback loops. - Spinoparabrachial Tract: Projects to the parabrachial area \rightarrow amy

section: C. Descending Modulation, Endogenous Analgesia & DNIC/CPM
text: - PAG-RVM Axis (Periaqueductal Gray \rightarrow Rostroventromedial Medulla \rightarrow Dorsal Horn): - High density of endogenous opioid peptides (endorphins, enkephalins, dynorphins) and \mu -opioid receptors. - RVM Neurons: - OFF-cells: Display a burst of firing immediately preceding analgesia; inhibit spinal nociceptive transmission. Activated by opioids and cannabinoids. - ON-cells: Display a burst of firing immediately preceding nociceptive reflexes; facilitate spinal nociceptive transmission. Inactivated by opioids. - NEUTRAL-cells: Fire continuously without modulation. - Neurotransmitters: Descending inhibition uses Serotonin ( 5\text{-HT} via 5\text{-HT} 1 receptors) and Noradrenaline (from Locus Coeruleus via \alpha 2 -adrenergic receptors). - Diffuse Noxious Inhibitory Controls (DNIC / CPM - Conditioned Pain Modulation): - Principle: "Pain inhibits pain" — application of a conditioning noxious stimulus at a remote body region (e.g., hand in ice water) inhibits pain perception from a local test stimulus (e.g., pressure algometry on the leg). - Anatomical Circuit: Spino-bulbo-spinal loop mediated through the subnucleus reticularis dorsalis (SRD) in the caudal medulla. - Clinical Significance: Deficient or absent CPM is a hallmark of central sensitization and predicts post-surgical chronification (Yarnitsky 2012).

section: D. Peripheral vs. Central Sensitization & Wind-Up (1.1.4)
text: - Peripheral Sensitization: - Primary hyperalgesia confined to the site of tissue injury. - Mediated by the "inflammatory soup" ( \text{PGE} 2 , bradykinin, serotonin, histamine, NGF, \text{H}^+ , \text{IL}-1\beta, \text{TNF}-\alpha ). - Nociceptor transduction threshold is lowered; spontaneous firing occurs. - The "Wind-Up" Phenomenon (Homosynaptic Frequency-Dependent Summation): - Location: Spinal dorsal horn WDR neurons. - Trigger: Repetitive, low-frequency ( 0.5\text{–}2\text{ Hz} ) stimulation of peripheral unmyelinated C -fibers. - Mechanism: Slow clearance of Substance P and CGRP causes sustained depolarization, opening the Mg^{2+} gate on NMDA receptors. - Characteristics: Homosynaptic (confined to the stimulated pathway); Short duration (abates seconds after stimulus stops). - Human Psychophysical Correlate: Temporal Summation of Pain (TSP) . - Central Sensitization (Heterosynaptic Long-Term Potentiation / LTP): - Location & Target Neurons: Central nociceptive neurons (never peripheral afferents) — primarily spinal dorsal horn lamina V Wide Dynamic Range (WDR) and lamina I nociceptive-specific (NS) projection neurons, plus lamina II excitatory/inhibitory interneurons; also involves supraspinal amplification (RVM ON-cell facilitation, thalamus, limbic/cortical networks). - Mechanism: Massive intracellular calcium influx via unblocked NMDA receptors \rightarrow activation of Protein Kinase C ( PKC ), Calcium/Calmodulin-dependent kinase II ( CaMKII ), and MAP kinase pat

section: Diagnostic Criteria for Nociplastic Pain (Kosek et al. 2021 / EFIC Master Standard):
text: To classify musculoskeletal pain as nociplastic , the patient must meet: 1. Pain duration \ge 3\text{ months} (chronic). 2. Pain distribution is regional or multifocal / widespread rather than discrete. 3. Pain cannot be entirely explained by identifiable nociceptive or neuropathic mechanisms. 4. Clinical signs of pain hypersensitivity (at least one): - Evoked pain hypersensitivity (dynamic mechanical allodynia, static allodynia, cold/heat allodynia, or pinprick hyperalgesia). 5. History of pain hypersensitivity and presence of comorbid symptoms (at least one): - Extreme sensitivity to sound, light, or odors. - Sleep disturbance with frequent nocturnal awakenings. - Severe fatigue. - Cognitive dysfunction (concentration difficulties, memory lapses). ---

section: A. IASP Taxonomy (2020 Definitions)
text: - Pain: An unpleasant sensory and emotional experience associated with, or resembling that associated with, actual or potential tissue damage. (Note: Pain and nociception are different phenomena; pain cannot be inferred solely from sensory activity). - Allodynia: Pain due to a stimulus that does not normally provoke pain. - Hyperalgesia: Increased pain from a stimulus that normally provokes pain. - Hypoalgesia: Diminished pain in response to a normally painful stimulus. - Analgesia: Absence of pain in response to stimulation which would normally be painful. - Hyperpathia: A painful syndrome characterized by an abnormally painful reaction to a stimulus, especially a repetitive stimulus, as well as an increased threshold. - Dysesthesia: An unpleasant abnormal sensation, whether spontaneous or evoked. - Paresthesia: An abnormal sensation, whether spontaneous or evoked (unlike dysesthesia, not unpleasant). - Neuropathy: A disturbance of function or pathological change in a nerve. - Neuralgia: Pain in the distribution of a nerve or nerves.

section: B. ICD-11 Chronic Pain Classification (Treede et al. / WHO MG30)
text: ICD-11 divides chronic pain ( \ge 3\text{ months} ) into: 1. MG30.0 Chronic Primary Pain: - Pain in one or more anatomical regions that persists for >3 months and is associated with significant emotional distress or functional disability, and cannot be better explained by another chronic condition. - Subtypes: Chronic widespread pain (Fibromyalgia), Complex Regional Pain Syndrome (CRPS), Chronic primary headache/orofacial pain, Chronic primary visceral pain, Chronic primary musculoskeletal pain (e.g., non-specific CLBP). 2. MG30.1–MG30.6 Chronic Secondary Pain (Pain is secondary to an underlying disease entity): - MG30.1 Chronic Cancer-Related Pain (due to tumor progression or cancer therapy). - MG30.2 Chronic Post-Surgical or Post-Traumatic Pain (CPSP) . - MG30.3 Chronic Neuropathic Pain (peripheral or central). - MG30.4 Chronic Secondary Headache and Orofacial Pain (e.g., TMD, cervicogenic, giant cell arteritis). - MG30.5 Chronic Secondary Visceral Pain (e.g., Crohn's disease, endometriosis). - MG30.6 Chronic Secondary Musculoskeletal Pain (e.g., rheumatoid arthritis, structural spondylolisthesis, OA). ---

section: A. Multidimensional Domains (1.3.1)
text: - Sensory-Discriminative: Location, spatial extent, intensity, quality (throbbing, burning, aching). - Affective-Motivational: Threat value, fear, unpleasantness, distress, avoidance motivation. - Cognitive-Evaluative: Catastrophizing, meaning attributed to pain, self-efficacy, expectation, beliefs about damage. - Socio-Cultural: Family dynamics, workplace ergonomics, socioeconomic status, ethnic health disparities, insurance/litigation systems.

section: 📄 Paper 1: Malfliet et al. (2017) — Brain Changes & Cognitive-Emotional Factors
text: - Citation: Malfliet A, Coppieters I, et al. Eur J Pain , 2017. - Systematic Review of 28 MRI Studies: - High pain catastrophizing correlates directly with gray matter atrophy in the Dorsolateral Prefrontal Cortex (DLPFC) ( r = -0.66 ). Because the DLPFC normally provides top-down inhibitory control over limbic areas, thinning directly impairs descending pain inhibition. - Resting-state fMRI shows hyperconnectivity between medial PFC and the Default Mode Network (DMN) , demonstrating perpetual pain rumination during rest. - Plasticity: Successful CBT and pain neuroscience education reverse DLPFC gray matter thinning.

Affective-Motivational / Salience: Anterior Insula, ACC, amygdala, fronto-striatal loops. 3. Cognitive-Evaluative / Executive: Prefrontal cortex (DLPFC, OFC). 4. Reward / Valuation Circuit: Ventral Tegmental Area (VTA), Nucleus Accumbens (NAc). Chronic pain causes an allostatic shift: blunted natural reward (anhedonia) and dominance of pain avoidance.

section: 📄 Paper 3A: Le Bars, Mouraux, & Plaghki (2017) — Peripheral Mechanisms & Psychophysiology
text: - Citation: Le Bars D, Mouraux A, Plaghki L. Physiologie de la douleur : aspects psychophysiologiques et mécanismes périphériques. EMC - Anesthésie-Réanimation 2017; Article 36-020-A-10 . - Core Scope & Exam Essentials (Official EFIC Mandatory Reading): - High-Threshold Transducers: Nociceptors are specialized physiological sensory transducers responding exclusively to actual or potential tissue-damaging stimuli (thermal >43^\circ\text{C} , mechanical, chemical), NOT non-specific general receptors pushed to high intensity. - First vs. Second Pain Kinetics: Rapid mechanical/thermal pricking pain conveyed by lightly myelinated A\delta fibers ( 5\text{–}30\text{ m/s} ) vs. slow, burning, poorly localized second pain conveyed by unmyelinated C fibers ( 0.5\text{–}2\text{ m/s} ). - Neurogenic Flare & Axon Reflex: Antidromic depolarization of peptidergic C -fibers causes peripheral release of CGRP (arteriolar vasodilation / flare) and Substance P (plasma extravasation / wheal/edema) without requiring central spinal activation. - Studiegids Verwijzing: Integraal uitgewerkt in Sectie 2.A (Primary Afferents & Peripheral Sensors) hierboven. ---

section: 📄 Paper 3B: Mouraux, Plaghki, & Le Bars (2017) — Central Mechanisms & Descending Controls
text: - Citation: Mouraux A, Plaghki L, Le Bars D. Physiologie de la douleur : mécanismes centraux et contrôles. EMC - Anesthésie-Réanimation 2017; Article 36-020-A-20 . - Core Scope & Exam Essentials (Official EFIC Mandatory Reading): - Dual Ascending Routing: - Neospinothalamic tract: Laminae I & V \rightarrow lateral thalamus (VPL/VPI) \rightarrow primary and secondary somatosensory cortices ( S1, S2 ); encodes sensory-discriminative properties (location, intensity, duration). - Paleospinothalamic / Spinoreticulothalamic tract: Laminae I, V, VII, VIII \rightarrow medial thalamus, reticular formation, and parabrachial nucleus \rightarrow anterior insula and anterior cingulate cortex (ACC); encodes affective-motivational unpleasantness and motor alerting. - Wide Dynamic Range (WDR) Neurons (Lamina V): Neurons that receive convergent monosynaptic input from non-noxious A\beta mechanoreceptors and polysynaptic input from A\delta and C fibers. Subject to wind-up via progressive NMDA receptor activation upon repeated C-fiber firing ( 0.5\text{–}2\text{ Hz} ). - Diffuse Noxious Inhibitory Controls (DNIC): Discovered by Le Bars (1979). A unique spino-bulbo-spinal negative feedback loop: noxious conditioning input anywhere on the body activates the subnucleus reticularis dorsalis (SRD) in the caudal medulla, sending descending non-opioid/noradrenergic inhibitory signals to silence all other dorsal horn WDR neurons outside the conditioning field ("pain inhibits pain"). - Studiegids Verwij

section: Section 2: Principles of Assessment and Measurement — EFIC Ingest & Study Guide
text: This module synthesizes the clinical frameworks, diagnostic grading criteria, mechanism-based classifications, psychometric measurement tools, and physical examination protocols required for Section Two: Principles of Assessment and Measurement of the official EFIC Core Curriculum. ---

section: A. WHO International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF)
text: The EFIC curriculum mandates the application of the ICF model to pain physiotherapy assessment: - Body Functions & Structures ( b/s ): Nociceptive processing, central sensitization, range of motion, muscle strength, joint stability, structural lesions, sleep architecture. - Activities ( d ): Walking tolerance, lifting, bending, sitting tolerance, self-care, stairs, dressing. - Participation ( d ): Paid employment, household roles, recreational pursuits, family life, community engagement. - Environmental Factors ( e ): Physical workplace setup, ergonomic demands, insurance policies, clinical invalidation vs. social support, assistive technology. - Personal Factors: Age, sex/gender, coping style, catastrophizing, fear-avoidance beliefs, pain self-efficacy, health literacy, adverse childhood experiences (ACEs).

section: B. Neuropathic Pain: Updated Diagnostic Grading System (Finnerup et al. 2016)
text: Paper: Finnerup NB, Haroutounian S, Kamerman P, Baron R, Bennett DL, et al. Neuropathic pain: an updated grading system for research and clinical practice. Pain, 2016.

section: The 4-Step Neuropathic Diagnostic Algorithm:
text: 1. Plausible Neuroanatomical Distribution: Pain distribution is neuroanatomically plausible (e.g., peripheral nerve territory, dermatomal, or central somatotopic distribution). 2. Relevant History: History suggestive of a relevant lesion or disease affecting the somatosensory nervous system (e.g., stroke, spinal cord injury, herpes zoster, radiculopathy, diabetic polyneuropathy). 3. Confirmed Negative/Positive Sensory Signs: Clinical sensory examination demonstrates negative signs (sensory loss: hypoesthesia, hypoalgesia) and/or positive signs (allodynia, hyperalgesia) confined strictly to the neuroanatomically plausible area. 4. Diagnostic Test Confirmation: Objective diagnostic test confirming lesion/disease of somatosensory system (e.g., MRI/CT imaging confirming nerve root compression, EMG/nerve conduction studies confirming axonal loss, skin biopsy showing reduced intraepidermal nerve fiber density).

section: Grading Levels (Crucial for EFIC MCQs):
text: - Possible Neuropathic Pain: Criteria (1) + (2) met (plausible distribution + relevant history). No physical examination or confirmatory tests yet performed. - Probable Neuropathic Pain: Criteria (1) + (2) + (3) met (plausible distribution + relevant history + clinical sensory examination confirms signs). - Definite Neuropathic Pain: Criteria (1) + (2) + (3) + (4) met (all criteria met including objective diagnostic test). ---

section: C. Mechanism-Based Musculoskeletal Pain Classification (Smart et al. 2011)
text:
Paper: Smart KM, Blake C, Staines A, Doody C. The Discriminative validity of "nociceptive," "peripheral neuropathic," and "central sensitization" as mechanisms-based classifications of musculoskeletal pain. Clin J Pain, 2011. Smart et al. established validated clinical indicator clusters that discriminate between three primary mechanisms: Mechanism Defining Clinical Features (Clusters) --- --- Nociceptive Pain • Pain localized to area of injury/dysfunction.
• Clear, proportionate mechanical / anatomical pattern of aggravation and easing.
• Intermittent, sharp with movement or dull ache at rest.
• Absence of dysesthesia, burning, or allodynia.
• Pain resolves or fluctuates predictably with physical loading. Peripheral Neuropathic Pain • Pain referred in a dermatomal or cutaneous nerve distribution.
• History of nerve injury, pathology, or mechanical compromise.
• Pain provocable with neurodynamic tests (SLR, ULNT) and nerve trunk palpation.
• Positive symptoms: burning, shooting, electric shocks, hyperalgesia.
• Negative symptoms: numbness, sensory loss, motor weakness/reflex changes. Central Sensitization Pain • Disproportionate, non-mechanical, unpredictable pattern of pain aggravation.
• Widespread, diffuse pain distribution not conforming to anatomical pathways.
• Hyperalgesia and/or allodynia across broad areas (secondary hyperalgesia).
• Presence of psychosocial symptoms: severe fatigue, unrefreshing sleep, cognitive difficulties, sensory

section: D. Neurodynamic Testing & Structural Differentiation
text: - Straight Leg Raise (SLR) Mechanics: Stresses the sciatic nerve, lumbosacral nerve roots (L4–S2), and dura mater. - Sensitizing Maneuvers (Increase Neural Strain): - Ankle dorsiflexion + eversion ( Bragard's test / tibial nerve bias). - Ankle plantarflexion + inversion ( fibular / common peroneal nerve bias ). - Ankle dorsiflexion + inversion ( sural nerve bias ). - Hip adduction and hip medial (internal) rotation. - Cervical and trunk flexion (Slump / Soto-Hall maneuver). - Desensitizing / Slackening Maneuvers (Decrease Neural Strain): - Knee flexion: Completely slacks the sciatic nerve. If distal radiating leg symptoms immediately abate when the knee is slightly flexed, it confirms neurogenic rather than muscular (hamstring) origin. - Ankle neutral/plantarflexion; hip external rotation and abduction. - Upper Limb Neurodynamic Tests (ULNT): - ULNT1 (Median nerve bias): Shoulder depression, abduction to 110^\circ , wrist/finger extension, forearm supination, shoulder external rotation, elbow extension. Sensitizing: contralateral cervical lateral flexion. - ULNT2A (Median nerve bias - alternative): Scapular depression, elbow extension, lateral rotation, wrist extension. - ULNT2B (Radial nerve bias): Scapular depression, elbow extension, shoulder internal rotation, forearm pronation, wrist flexion + ulnar deviation. - ULNT3 (Ulnar nerve bias): Wrist extension + radial deviation, forearm pronation, elbow flexion, shoulder external rotation, shoulder depression, abduction to 90^

section: 1. Headache and Orofacial Pain:
text: - Cervicogenic Headache (CGH - IHS / Sjaastad Criteria): - Unilateral headache without side shift, radiating from occipital region to fronto-temporal areas. - Aggravated by specific neck movements or sustained awkward postures. - Provoked by manual palpation of ipsilateral upper cervical facet joints ( C1\text{–}C3 ). - Flexion-Rotation Test (FRT): High diagnostic accuracy (sensitivity 90%, specificity 90%). Normal rotation in full cervical flexion is \approx 44^\circ to each side. A restriction of \ge 10^\circ to the symptomatic side indicates C1\text{–}C2 dysfunction. - Temporomandibular Disorders (DC-TMD Criteria): - Pain in jaw, temple, in front of the ear, or inside the ear. - Aggravated by jaw motion (chewing, yawning, speaking). - Replication of familiar pain on palpation of masseter or temporalis muscles (myofascial TMD) or temporomandibular joint capsule (arthralgia). - Joint sounds (clicking = disc displacement with reduction; crepitus = osteoarthritis / degenerative joint disease).

section: 2. Chronic Pelvic Pain (CPPS, Endometriosis, Vulvodynia):
text: - Assessment Components: - Screen for red flags (unexplained hematuria, rectal bleeding, post-menopausal bleeding, pelvic masses). - Visceral-somatic convergence: Chronic visceral irritation (endometriosis, interstitial cystitis) triggers secondary pelvic floor hypertonicity, spasm, and cutaneous allodynia over T10–S4 dermatomes. - Musculoskeletal assessment: Lumbopelvic stability, hip mobility, external pelvic palpation (obturator internus, pubic symphysis, sacroiliac joints), and gentle internal myofascial assessment (when certified). - Trauma-informed care: High prevalence of psychological trauma, sexual abuse history, or medical trauma; mandatory explicit consent and patient control over examination.

section: 3. Visceral Pain & Somatic Referral:
text: - Characterized by dull, diffuse, poorly localized aching often accompanied by autonomic responses (nausea, diaphoresis, pallor, bradycardia/tachycardia). - Mediated by convergent visceral and somatic afferents onto wide dynamic range (WDR) neurons in lamina V of the dorsal horn. - Elicits secondary somatic hyperalgesia and muscle guarding in corresponding dermatomes/myotomes (e.g., gallbladder referring to right shoulder / C3-C5 via phrenic nerve; cardiac ischemia referring to left inner arm / T1-T2). ---

section: F. Health Literacy, Stigma & Diagnostic Uncertainty (Curriculum 1.2.2 & 2.1.4)
text: - Health Literacy Principles: - Dynamic and modifiable; health literacy is a bidirectional clinical property, not just a patient deficit. - Teach-Back Method: Asking the patient to summarize the management plan in their own words; identifies cognitive gaps without patronizing. - Use of plain language: Replace catastrophic biomedical framing ("bone-on-bone", "crumbling spine", "slipped disc") with reassuring biopsychosocial metaphors ("sensitive car alarm", "protective muscle splinting", "robust joint resilience"). - Navigating Diagnostic Uncertainty (When Tests are Normal): - Validating the reality of the patient's suffering ( "Your pain is 100% real" ). - Explaining the limitation of structural imaging ( "Scans show anatomy, like a photograph, but they cannot show how the volume control of the nervous system is set" ). - De-stigmatizing nociplastic pain by validating neurobiological changes (central sensitization, cortical reorganization) without resorting to psychogenic dismissal. ---

section: 📄 Paper 4: Fillingim, Loeser, Baron, & Edwards (2016) — Assessment Domains & Methods
text: Citation: Fillingim RB, Loeser JD, Baron R, Edwards RR. Assessment of Chronic Pain: Domains, Methods, and Mechanisms. J Pain. 2016 Sep;17(9 Suppl):T10-26. - The IMMPACT / ACTTION Core Outcome Domains for Chronic Pain: 1. Pain Intensity: Measured dynamically (at rest, on movement, worst, average over 7 days). 2. Physical Functioning: Multidimensional assessment of mobility, daily activities, role functioning. 3. Emotional Functioning: Depressive symptoms, anxiety, anger, pain catastrophizing. 4. Participant Ratings of Global Improvement: Patient Global Impression of Change (PGIC) (7-point Likert scale). 5. Symptoms and Adverse Events: Treatment tolerability, side effects. 6. Participant Disposition: Adherence, study completion/dropouts. - Quantitative Sensory Testing (QST - DFNS Protocol): - Standardized somatosensory phenotyping evaluating thermal thresholds (CDT, WDT, TSL, CPT, HPT), mechanical detection (MDT via von Frey filaments), mechanical pain threshold (MPT via pinprick), mechanical pain sensitivity (MPS), dynamic mechanical allodynia (DMA via brush), wind-up ratio (WUR), and vibration detection (VDT via tuning fork). - Detects sensory loss (neuropathic axonal injury) vs. sensory gain (hyperalgesia/allodynia indicating peripheral or central sensitization). ---

section: 📄 Paper 5: Faculty of Pain Medicine (FPM) & British Pain Society (BPS) 2019 — Outcome Measures
text: Citation: Faculty of Pain Medicine & British Pain Society. Outcome Measures. Royal College of Anaesthetists, 2019. - Core Minimum Dataset for Chronic Pain Audit: - Pain Severity & Interference: Brief Pain Inventory (BPI) . Assesses pain intensity (4 items) and interference with 7 life domains (general activity, mood, walking ability, normal work, relationships, sleep, enjoyment of life). - Health-Related Quality of Life: EQ-5D (EuroQol 5 Dimensions: Mobility, Self-Care, Usual Activities, Pain/Discomfort, Anxiety/Depression + EQ-VAS 0–100). - Psychological Distress: HADS (Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale) or PHQ-9 (depression) / GAD-7 (anxiety). - Pain Self-Efficacy: PSEQ (Pain Self-Efficacy Questionnaire) : 10 items, scored 0–60. Higher scores ( >40 ) reflect strong confidence in performing activities despite pain; scores <30 predict poor engagement and high disability. - Kinesiophobia: TSK (Tampa Scale for Kinesiophobia) : 17 items, score 17–68; scores >37 indicate high fear of movement. - Catastrophizing: PCS (Pain Catastrophizing Scale) : 13 items, score 0–52; scores \ge 30 indicate clinically relevant catastrophizing (subscales: Rumination, Magnification, Helplessness). ---

section: 📄 Paper 6: Wang et al. (2016) — Persistent Post-Surgical Pain Predictors
text: Citation: Wang L, Guyatt GH, Kennedy SA, et al. Predictors of persistent pain after breast cancer surgery: a systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies. CMAJ. 2016;188(14):E352-E361. - Quantitative Predictors of Chronification (Persistent Post-Surgical Pain / PPSP): 1. Axillary Lymph Node Dissection (ALND): Strongest independent surgical predictor ( \text{OR} = 2.41 , 95% CI 1.73–3.35) due to intercostobrachial nerve damage. Sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) carries significantly lower risk. 2. Younger Age: Each decade decrease in age increases PPSP risk ( \text{OR} = 1.36 ). 3. Radiotherapy: Significantly increases risk ( \text{OR} = 1.35 ) via chronic microvascular ischemia and radiation fibrosis. 4. Acute Post-Operative Pain: Severe acute pain within 24–72 hours post-surgery increases risk ( \text{OR} = 1.16\text{ per }1\text{-point increase} on 0–10 scale). 5. Preoperative Psychological Factors: High catastrophizing, state anxiety, and depression. 6. Surgical Scope: In contrast to ALND, the extent of breast tissue resection (mastectomy vs. breast-conserving lumpectomy) and adjuvant chemotherapy showed NO significant association with PPSP risk. ---

section: 📄 Paper 7: Verbunt, Huijnen, & Seelen (2012) — Objective Activity Monitoring
text: Citation: Verbunt JA, Huijnen IP, Seelen HA. Assessment of physical activity by movement registration systems in chronic pain: methodological considerations. Clin J Pain. 2012;28(6):496-504. - Central Findings: 1. Subjective vs. Objective Divergence: Patient self-reported physical activity (diaries/questionnaires) correlates poorly with objective movement registration systems (accelerometers, pedometers). Self-reports reflect pain severity and emotional distress rather than actual movement quantity. 2. Activity Subgroups in Chronic Pain: - Avoiders: Low physical activity, fearful of movement, leading to deconditioning. - Persisters / Over-activity (Boom-Bust): High intensity bursts on good days followed by prolonged flare-ups and immobility. 3. Methodological Requirements: Accelerometry requires multi-day monitoring (at least 4–7 consecutive days , including weekdays and weekends) to reliably capture habitual physical activity patterns. ---

section: 📄 Paper 8: Tyson & Brown (2014) — Pain Measurement in Neurological Conditions

section: 📄 Paper 9: Gordon (2015) — Acute Pain Assessment Beyond Simple Ratings
text: Citation: Gordon DB. Acute pain assessment tools: let us move beyond simple pain ratings. Curr Opin Anaesthesiol. 2015;28(5):565-9. - Key Takeaways for MCQ: 1. Limitations of Unidimensional Scales: Relying solely on 0–10 NRS at rest leads to over-reliance on opioids, ignores dynamic functional impairment, and fails to evaluate recovery. 2. Functional Pain Assessment: Pain MUST be assessed during functional activities (e.g., deep breathing, coughing, turning in bed, walking) rather than static resting pain alone. 3. Clinically Meaningful Difference (MCID): A reduction of \ge 2 points or \ge 30\% on the 0–10 NRS represents a clinically important difference in acute and chronic pain. 4. section: Section 3: Principles of Treatment — EFIC Ingest & Study Guide
text: This module covers the core clinical interventions, Cochrane review evidence bases, mechanism-based therapies, exercise neurobiology, digital health management, and multidisciplinary strategies for Section Three: Principles of Treatment of the official EFIC Core Curriculum. ---

section: A. Contextual Factors, Placebo & Nocebo in Physiotherapy (3.2 & 3.3)
text: Paper: Testa M, Rossettini G. Enhance placebo, avoid nocebo: How contextual factors affect physiotherapy outcomes. Man Ther. 2016 Aug;24:65-74. - The 5 Clusters of Contextual Factors (CFs) in Physiotherapy: 1. Physiotherapist Characteristics: Professional dress, demonstrated clinical competence, warm empathetic tone, non-verbal open posture, eye contact, gender concordance/preference. 2. Patient Characteristics: Positive treatment expectations, optimism, prior treatment experiences, internal locus of control. 3. Patient-Physiotherapist Relationship (Therapeutic Alliance): Shared decision making, deep listening, genuine empathy, therapeutic touch, validation of suffering. 4. Treatment Characteristics: Rituals of manual examination, visible modern therapeutic equipment, overt diagnostic labeling, convincing therapeutic narrative. 5. Healthcare Environment: Clean, calm, aesthetically welcoming clinic space, private treatment rooms, clear directional signage. - Clinical & Ethical Application: - Contextual factors are not noise — they are active, neurobiologically mediated drivers of clinical outcomes ( g \approx 0.5\text{–}0.7 ). - Placebo Mechanisms: Mediated by prefrontal expectation, release of endogenous opioids and endocannabinoids , and suppression of the limbic salience network (ACC/insula). - Nocebo Triggers to Eliminate: Avoid alarming biomechanical language ("your spine is wearing out", "bone-on-bone", "your pelvis is crooked"), dismissive communication, or indifferent

section: B. Nocebo Hyperalgesia Meta-Analysis (Petersen et al. 2014)
text: Paper: Petersen GL, Finnerup NB, Colloca L, et al. The magnitude of nocebo effects in pain: a meta-analysis. Pain. 2014 Aug;155(8):1426-34. - Core Findings: - Nocebo hyperalgesia has a moderate-to-large effect size . - Negative verbal suggestions paired with conditioning generate the largest effects ( g = 0.77 ), but negative verbal suggestion alone induces significant hyperalgesia ( g = 0.52 ). - Neurochemical Mechanism: Driven by anxiety and the cholecystokinin (CCK) system; completely reversible with the CCK antagonist proglumide .

section: C. Pain Neuroscience Education (PNE) & Patient Education (3.4)
text: - Moseley & Butler (2015) — 15 Years of Explaining Pain: - PNE reconceptualizes pain: shifts patient beliefs from pain as a marker of tissue pathology to pain as a marker of perceived danger/threat . - PNE reduces pain catastrophizing, kinesiophobia, healthcare overutilization, and sick leave. - Clinical Rule: Standalone PNE improves beliefs and catastrophizing, but must be combined with active movement / physical exercise to significantly reduce physical disability and restore function. - Geneen et al. (2015) Systematic Review: Pain biology education achieves moderate increases in pain knowledge and reductions in catastrophizing. - Engers et al. (2008) Cochrane Review on LBP Education: - Acute LBP: Brief patient education (e.g., The Back Book , reassurance that back pain is common and benign, advice to stay active) reduces sick leave and primary care consultations. - Chronic LBP: Brief generic advice is ineffective ; requires comprehensive, individualized biopsychosocial education. ---

section: B. Graded Activity vs. Graded Exposure (Macedo et al. 2010 & Linton et al. 2018)
text: - Macedo et al. (2010) Systematic Review: - Graded Activity (Operant Conditioning / Fordyce): - Focuses on functional quota setting . - Progression is strictly time-contingent , NOT pain-contingent. - Extinguishes pain behaviors (grimacing, moaning, resting) by withholding attention, while positively reinforcing healthy activity quotas. - Graded Exposure (In Vivo Cognitive-Behavioral Exposure / Vlaeyen): - Focuses on expectational threat violation . - Uses the PHODA (Photographs of Daily Activities) or fear hierarchy to identify specifically feared movements (e.g., lifting with a rounded spine). - Patients engage in the feared movement in a graded manner to disconfirm catastrophic expectations ( "I predicted my spine would snap, but I bent forward and it did not" ). - Comparative Outcome: Graded exposure produces greater reductions in catastrophizing and kinesiophobia in highly fearful patients. - Linton, Flink, & Vlaeyen (2018) — Psychological Etiology of Pain: - Pain behaviors develop through Pavlovian respondent conditioning (innocuous proprioceptive sensations become conditioned stimuli eliciting fear) and operant conditioning. - Avoidance acts as a safety behavior: While avoidance temporarily relieves fear (negative reinforcement), it prevents the extinction of threat expectations and guarantees physical deconditioning.

section: C. Acceptance and Mindfulness-Based Interventions (Veehof et al. 2016)
text: Paper: Veehof MM, Oskam M, Schreurs KM, Bohlmeijer ET. Acceptance- and mindfulness-based interventions for the treatment of chronic pain: a meta-analytic review. Cogn Behav Ther. 2016;45(1):5-31. - Evidence Quality: Low-to-high quality across 25 RCTs. - Effect Sizes by Outcome: - Moderate effect: Specifically on pain interference and anxiety . - Small effect: On pain intensity , depression , and disability . - Core Principle: ACT focuses on psychological flexibility and value-based living in the presence of pain , rather than trying to eliminate pain sensations. ---

section: A. Central Mechanisms of Exercise-Induced Analgesia & Hyperalgesia
text: Paper: Lima LV, Abner TSS, Sluka KA. Does exercise increase or decrease pain? Central mechanisms underlying these two phenomena. J Physiol. 2017 Jul 1;595(13):4141-4150. Paper: Sluka KA, Frey-Law L, Hoeger Bement M. Exercise-induced pain and analgesia? Underlying mechanisms and clinical translation. Pain. 2018 Sep;159 Suppl 1:S91-S97. - Exercise-Induced Hypoalgesia (EIH) in Healthy Individuals: - Acute bouts of exercise increase pain thresholds locally and systemically. - Mechanisms: 1. Endogenous Opioidergic System: Upregulation of \mu -opioid receptor activation in the Rostroventromedial Medulla (RVM) and Periaqueductal Gray (PAG). Blocked by naloxone. 2. Endocannabinoid System: Circulating anandamide and 2-AG levels increase during sustained aerobic exercise ( >60\%\ \text{VO} 2\text{max} ), acting via CB 1 receptors. 3. Serotonergic and Noradrenergic Descending Inhibition: Increases dorsal horn serotonin ( 5\text{-HT} 1A ) and noradrenaline ( \alpha 2 -adrenergic receptors). 4. Anti-inflammatory Cytokines: Contracting skeletal muscle releases "myokines" (particularly \text{IL}-6 , which stimulates anti-inflammatory \text{IL}-10 and \text{IL}-1\text{ra} and inhibits \text{TNF}-\alpha ). - Exercise-Induced Hyperalgesia in Chronic / Nociplastic Pain: - Patients with fibromyalgia, chronic fatigue syndrome, and severe central sensitization often experience a paradoxical worsening of pain following exercise. - Why? 1. section: B. Clinical Evidence Across Exercise Modalities
text: - Geneen et al. (2017) Cochrane Overview: Physical activity and exercise produce consistent, statistically significant reductions in pain and disability across all chronic musculoskeletal conditions; safe, low adverse event profile. - Bidonde et al. (2017) Cochrane Review (Fibromyalgia): Aerobic exercise training improves health-related quality of life ( \text{MD} = -5.6/100 ), physical function ( \text{MD} = -6.4/100 ), and pain ( \text{MD} = -8.8/100 ) with moderate-quality evidence. - Searle et al. (2015) Meta-Analysis (CLBP): Motor control exercise and resistance training show slightly superior short-term pain relief, but long-term functional equivalence across all active exercise modalities. ---

section: A. Efficacy of Internet-Delivered Interventions
text: - Eccleston et al. (2014) Cochrane Review — Internet-Delivered Psychological Therapies for Chronic Pain: - Evaluated 15 RCTs in adults. - Disability: Moderate reduction at post-treatment. - Pain Intensity: Small reduction. - Depression & Anxiety: Small-to-moderate improvements. - Critical Finding: Therapist-guided internet interventions are substantially more effective than unguided, automated self-help programs.

section: B. Wearables & Electronic Activity Feedback
text: - Oliveira et al. (2018) Systematic Review & Meta-Analysis (Arch Phys Med Rehabil): - Citation: Oliveira CB, Franco MR, Maher CG, et al. Physical Activity-Based Interventions Using Electronic Feedback May Be Ineffective in Reducing Pain and Disability in Patients With Chronic Musculoskeletal Pain. Arch Phys Med Rehabil. 2018 Sep;99(9):1900-1912. - Crucial MCQ Finding: Providing patients with electronic activity feedback alone (wearable pedometers, smartphone step counters, smartwatch alerts) does NOT significantly reduce pain or disability compared to minimal interventions. - Mechanism: Merely quantifying daily steps or activity without personalized behavioral counseling, biopsychosocial goal-setting, and pacing fails to alter pain beliefs or functional coping.

section: C. Telehealth & Virtual Reality (VR)
text: - Telehealth in Pain Physiotherapy: Effective for delivering exercise coaching, PNE, and remote monitoring; matches clinic-based outcomes for chronic low back and osteoarthritis pain when high therapeutic alliance is maintained. - Immersive Virtual Reality (VR): Acts via intense attentional distraction (reducing sensory-discriminative and insular BOLD signaling) and sensorimotor recalibration (providing visual illusion of painless limb excursion). Effective for acute procedural pain, burns, and CRPS motor retraining. ---

section: B. Neurobiological Mechanisms of Manual Therapy (Bialosky & Sluka Model)
text: - Foundational Source: Bialosky et al. (2009, 2018) / Sluka (ed.) Mechanisms and Management of Pain for the Physical Therapist (IASP Press). - Core Principle: Manual therapy produces hypoalgesia through a complex cascade of neurophysiological mechanisms , NOT merely structural realignment or "breaking up adhesions": 1. Segmental Spinaal (Spinal Mechanisms): - Mechanical input activates large-diameter A\beta mechanoreceptors. - Stimulates inhibitory interneurons in the dorsal horn (Lamina II / Substantia Gelatinosa), closing the gate to nociceptive input (Gate Control Theory). - Modulates motor neuron pool excitability, reducing localized protective muscle guarding. 2. Supraspinaal & Descenderend (Central Descending Control): - Stimulates brainstem centres, particularly the Periaqueductal Gray (PAG) and Rostral Ventromedial Medulla (RVM) . - Activates descending pain modulatory pathways mediated by endogenous opioids , serotonin ( 5\text{-HT} ), and noradrenaline ( \text{NA} ). - Generates widespread/systemic hypoalgesia (pain relief extends beyond the treated segment). 3. Perifeer & Weefselniveau (Tissue & Mechanical Factors): - Mechanotransductie: transient mechanical force influences local interstitial fluid dynamics, improves microcirculation, and modulates inflammatory mediators (downregulation of cytokines, CGRP, and Substance P), supporting tissue repair processes. 4. section: C. Complementary & Active Self-Care Therapies (Curriculum 3.10)
text: - Wieland et al. (2017) Cochrane Review — Yoga for Chronic Non-Specific LBP: - Low-to-moderate quality evidence that yoga produces small-to-moderate improvements in back-related function and pain compared to non-exercise controls; clinically equivalent to standard physical therapy exercise. - Patti et al. (2015) — Pilates for Chronic LBP: - Pilates exercise programs deliver small-to-moderate reductions in pain and disability; effective, but not superior to other active exercise forms. - Crawford et al. (2014) Pain Med — Active Self-Care CAM Therapies: - Evaluated mind-body CAM therapies (yoga, tai chi, meditation/mindfulness). Emphasizes that CAM therapies are most effective when they empower active patient engagement and self-efficacy rather than passive reliance on external providers. ---

section: A. Interdisciplinary Rehabilitation & Return to Work (RTW)
text: - Kamper et al. (2015) Cochrane / BMJ Review: - Intensive multidisciplinary biopsychosocial rehabilitation (physical conditioning + psychological CBT + workplace interventions) is superior to physical therapy alone or usual care . - Significantly increases the odds of returning to work at long-term follow-up ( >12\text{ months} ) with an Odds Ratio \mathbf{\text{OR} = 1.87} . - Gatchel et al. (2014) — Multidisciplinary vs. Interdisciplinary Teams: - Multidisciplinary: Clinicians from multiple disciplines work in parallel silos, with independent assessments and separate goals. - Interdisciplinary: Clinicians work as an integrated, collaborative team holding regular team conferences, resolving conflicting clinical messages, and sharing synchronized functional goals with the patient. Interdisciplinary care delivers superior outcomes and cost savings.

section: B. Physical Conditioning & Work Disability
text: - Schaafsma et al. (2013) Cochrane Review — Physical Conditioning Programs for Workers with Back Pain: - Work-focused physical conditioning programs reduce sick leave by an average of 45 fewer days at 12-month follow-up compared to usual care in workers on subacute/chronic sick leave. - Inclusion of actual workplace visits and ergonomic job modifications dramatically enhances RTW success. - Oesch et al. (2010) Systematic Review: High-intensity conditioning programs incorporating functional job simulation reduce work disability in non-acute non-specific LBP. ---

section: Section 4: Populations in Pain & Specific Conditions — EFIC Ingest & Study Guide
text: This module covers the epidemiology, evidence-based management, and specialized assessment protocols for Section Four: Populations in Pain of the official EFIC Core Curriculum. ---

section: A. Epidemiology of Chronic Pain in Europe (Curriculum 4.1)
text: - Prevalence: Chronic pain affects approximately 19\%\text{–}20\% of the European adult population (Breivik et al. 2006). - Demographic Predictors: Higher prevalence in females, advancing age, lower socioeconomic status, and manual labor occupations. - Societal Impact: One of the leading causes of years lived with disability (YLD) globally; direct medical costs and indirect productivity losses account for >1.5\text{–}3\% of European GDP.

section: B. Fibromyalgia & Chronic Widespread Pain (Curriculum 4.2.1)
text: - ACR 2010 / 2016 Diagnostic Criteria: - Diagnosed without requiring manual tender point examination. - Criteria met if: 1. Widespread Pain Index (WPI) \ge 7 and Symptom Severity Scale (SSS) \ge 5 , OR WPI 3–6 and SSS \ge 9 . 2. Generalized pain defined as pain in at least 4 out of 5 regions (left upper, right upper, left lower, right lower, and axial). 3. Symptoms present at a similar level for at least 3 months . 4. Diagnosis of fibromyalgia is valid irrespective of other diagnoses (does not exclude other clinical illnesses). - Core Pathophysiology: Prototype of nociplastic pain — characterized by reduced central descending inhibition (deficient CPM), heightened temporal summation of pain (TSP), elevated substance P and glutamate in CSF, and functional connectivity changes in the default mode network. - Evidence-Based Rehabilitation (EULAR Recommendations & Bidonde 2017): - First-line therapy: Graded aerobic exercise (moderate-quality Cochrane evidence; Bidonde 2017) and strength training. - Multicomponent therapy: Aerobic exercise + Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) + Pain Neuroscience Education (PNE). - Pharmacotherapy is secondary (duloxetine, milnacipran, pregabalin; opioids are strongly contraindicated).

section: C. Complex Regional Pain Syndrome (CRPS Types I & II) (Curriculum 4.2.2)
text: Papers: Smart KM, Wand BM, O'Connell NE. Cochrane Database Syst Rev , 2016; Méndez-Rebolledo G et al. J Back Musculoskelet Rehabil , 2017. - Diagnostic Distinction (Budapest Diagnostic Criteria): - CRPS Type I (Reflex Sympathetic Dystrophy): Develops after an initiating noxious event (fracture, sprain, surgery) or immobilization without verifiable major peripheral nerve injury . - CRPS Type II (Causalgia): Develops following identifiable major peripheral nerve injury (e.g., median or tibial nerve transection). - Budapest Diagnostic Categories (Must exhibit symptoms in \ge 3 categories and signs in \ge 2 categories): 1. Sensory: Hyperalgesia (to pinprick) and/or allodynia (to light touch/temperature/deep somatic pressure). 2. Vasomotor: Temperature asymmetry ( >1^\circ\text{C} ) and/or skin color changes / asymmetry. 3. Sudomotor / Edema: Edema and/or sweating changes / sweating asymmetry. 4. Motor / Trophic: Decreased range of motion and/or motor dysfunction (weakness, tremor, dystonia) and/or trophic changes (hair, nail, skin changes). - Evidence-Based Physiotherapy: - Graded Motor Imagery (GMI) & Mirror Therapy: Moderate-quality evidence for reducing pain and disability in CRPS 1. Must follow the strict sequence: (1) Laterality recognition \rightarrow (2) Imagined movements \rightarrow (3) Mirror therapy. - Tactile Sensory Discrimination: Touching varying textures or localization on skin restores somatotopic representation in S1 . - Clinical Warning: Aggressive passive stre
